notable_claims: Louisiana Tech University allegedly disabled student Internet email and monitored students' Netnews subscriptions.
The Electronic Frontier Foundation provided legal guidance for students whose computer privileges were suspended due to 'hacker newsletters'.
Debate exists over whether university administrations should close entire forums or specifically enforce anti-harassment rules.
classification.summary: This digest summarizes various discussions regarding academic freedom and censorship in university settings during September 1992. Key topics include a dispute over dorm-door postings at Iowa State University, allegations of email censorship at Louisiana Tech University, and the role of system administrators in balancing privacy with operational needs.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.47

notable_claims: The author argues that dormitory doors are not established free-speech forums and thus subject to university regulation.
The author suggests that closing a forum is preferable to lengthy disciplinary proceedings for harassment violations.
classification.summary: A debate between Wes Morgan and Carl M. Kadie regarding whether the administration of Iowa State University can legally prohibit students from posting materials on dormitory doors. Morgan argues that since dorm doors were not created as free-speech forums, the university has the right to close them to prevent harassment. Kadie contends that such actions constitute censorship similar to closing a student newspaper.
classification.title: Re: Censorship at Iowa State

notable_claims: Federal courts distinguish between harassing speech (which can be prohibited) and offensive speech (which is protected).
It is unconstitutional for state universities to base campus speech restrictions on EEOC rules.
Content-based prohibitions on speech, even if well-intended to address bigotry, generally cannot survive constitutional screening.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues against closing public forums to suppress offensive material, asserting that offensive speech is protected by the Constitution and academic freedom. He provides a curated list of legal precedents and EFF resources to distinguish between illegal harassment and protected expression in university settings. The post specifically addresses the application of these principles to Netnews and email.
classification.title: Re: Censorship at Iowa State

notable_claims: The presence of viewpoint discrimination is absolute evidence of an attempt to stifle expression.
A state university's contractual rights cannot supersede the US Constitution.
Universities may legally designate specific 'free speech areas' while restricting other public physical plants.
classification.summary: A discussion between Wes Morgan and J. S. Greenfield regarding the legality of restricting posters in university dormitories at Iowa State University. The participants debate whether such restrictions constitute censorship or legitimate 'time, place, and manner' restrictions on free speech within public areas of a state institution.
classification.title: Re: Censorship at Iowa State

notable_claims: Government regulation of speech must be content-neutral to serve a state interest.
Restrictions on government employee speech do not necessarily apply to university students.
Content-motivated speech restrictions are generally not permissible for government landlords in university housing.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to Wes Morgan regarding the legality of 'free speech areas' and censorship on university campuses. Using ACLU guidelines and legal precedents, Kadie argues that universities cannot restrict speech to specific 'ghettos' if those restrictions are content-motivated. The post also provides resources for researching academic freedom via EFF servers.
classification.title: Article 4--Re: Censorship at Iowa State

notable_claims: The ISU Department of Residence implemented a policy restricting postings on dorm doors following 'racist' and 'denegrating' posts.
The author claims the door policy is unconstitutional based on Tinker v Des Moines, RAV v. St Paul, Ward v. RAR, and Frisby v. Schultz.
classification.summary: Mark A. Anstrom provides updates on a censorship policy implemented by the Iowa State University Department of Residence regarding posting materials on dorm doors. He discusses the lack of transparency regarding a student committee formed to review the policy and mentions an editorial he wrote citing legal precedents to argue the policy is unconstitutional.
classification.title: More ISU Censorship info

notable_claims: Possession of hacker newsletters does not constitute computer intrusion.
Most sexually oriented Usenet newsgroups are protected expression under American Constitutional law rather than legal obscenity.
System administrators rummaging through student directories may violate students' rights.
classification.summary: An excerpt from the Electronic Frontier Foundation's publication detailing legal assistance for individuals facing computer-access suspensions and censorship. Mike Godwin highlights issues such as system administrators searching student directories and universities blocking Usenet newsgroups based on misconceptions of obscenity law.
classification.title: EFFector Online 3.05: EFF Legal Services

notable_claims: The Fighting Words doctrine is the basis for most college speech codes and hate speech laws.
In Rust v. Sullivan, the Court suggested universities have a unique tradition of free speech that distinguishes them from other government-funded entities.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie shares notes from a talk by Nat Hentoff at the University of Illinois regarding multiculturalism and free speech. The item discusses key Supreme Court cases like RAV v. St. Paul and Rust v. Sullivan, specifically noting how 'fighting words' doctrines often underpin college speech codes. It also provides a list of legal references available via EFF FTP servers.
classification.title: Article 7--"Multiculturalism and the First Amendment"

notable_claims: Louisiana Tech disabled student Internet email functions.
University individuals were allegedly reading students' mail and newsgroup subscriptions.
Students were reportedly penalized for reading 'offbeat' newsgroups.
classification.summary: A student reports that Louisiana Tech University disabled all student email functions for the Internet. The author alleges that university officials were monitoring students' Usenet subscriptions and using their reading habits as grounds for disciplinary action.
classification.title: Article 8--NICK=La. Tech=CENSORSHIP

notable_claims: Academic computing centers are shifting from providing raw resources to integrating them and shaping the community's vision of their use.
The proliferation of electronic formats has increased user ignorance regarding available information sources.
Information literacy requires a collaborative effort between libraries, computing centers, and faculty.
classification.summary: Calvin Boyer discusses the convergence of university libraries and academic computing centers in response to the proliferation of electronic information. He argues that both institutions must collaborate to provide 'information literacy' to faculty and students as traditional resource delivery models shift. The post highlights the challenge of mastering machine-dependent tools and protocols to ensure users can effectively exploit electronic resources.
classification.title: Article 9--libraries and computer centers

notable_claims: Universities that censor available information lose the respect normally afforded to them.
Institutional censorship persists because users do not challenge the administrators.
classification.summary: Steven S. Brack responds to a discussion regarding the censorship of 'alt.*' newsgroups on university systems. He argues that institutional censorship is permitted only because users fail to exercise control over administrators. Brack mentions being banned by administrators at Ohio State University as an example of such censorship.
classification.title: Article 10--Re: What do you do about alt.*

identity.subject: Article 10--Re: What do you do about alt.*

notable_claims: The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) maintained an archive of university computer use policies at ftp.eff.org/pub/academic/policies.
Privacy is defined as not looking at data, whereas confidentiality is the obligation not to disclose data seen during job duties.
There is no absolute right of privacy in a networked computing environment; it is a limited right balanced against operational needs.
The Electronic Communications Privacy Act and Federal Educational Records Privacy Act (FERPA) provide frameworks for balancing privacy and need-to-know access.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the drafting of a University Computer Use Policy at the University of Rochester. The exchange focuses on the tension between user privacy and the administrative need for system staff to access files for maintenance or policy enforcement. Joseph Watters advises distinguishing between 'privacy' (not looking) and 'confidentiality' (not disclosing), while noting that no absolute right to privacy exists in networked environments.
classification.title: Article 11--Re: Computer use policy document

notable_claims: System managers should not perform 'dragnets' or sweep through accounts without reasonable suspicion.
Computer search practices should be integrated into established institutional judicial procedures (e.g., student conduct boards).
Skidmore College policy requires prior consent to look at mail files, except when approved by a committee following suspected intrusion.
classification.summary: Leo Geoffrion outlines a computer use policy at Skidmore College that emphasizes the distinction between privacy and confidentiality. He argues against 'dragnets' by system managers and advocates for requiring reasonable suspicion and oversight from institutional review boards before searching user accounts. The described policy requires committee approval to examine mail files unless there is an immediate system crisis.
classification.title: Re: Computer use policy document
